lead: A seal keeps the oil in and the dirt, water and process fluid out. Every bearing in this unit needs one: a journal bearing loses its film if the oil leaks away, and a rolling bearing fails early once grit gets in. Static seals, such as gaskets and O-rings, close a joint between parts that do not move against each other; dynamic seals, such as lip seals, face seals and labyrinths, close the gap round a moving shaft. Designing a gasket joint means finding the bolt load that seats the gasket and keeps it tight under pressure.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for lubricants and Chapter 5.2 for the bearing types a seal protects.

blocks.text: A leak needs a path: the roughness between two bolted faces, or the running clearance round a shaft. A contact seal fills the path with a soft material pressed hard against both faces; a clearance seal makes it so long and narrow that little fluid gets through.

items: Gasket: a flat ring of compressible material clamped between flanges by bolts, on pipe flanges, pump casings and covers.
O-ring: an elastomer ring of round section squeezed in a groove, in a cover joint or on a slowly moving rod.
Lip seal (oil seal): a rubber lip held on the shaft by a garter spring, facing the oil; the standard gearbox and motor shaft seal.
Mechanical face seal: a spring presses a rotating carbon ring against a fixed ring of silicon carbide or ceramic, both lapped flat; used on pumps.
Labyrinth seal: fins with a small running gap and no contact. It never wears and suits steam turbines, but always leaks a little.
Gland packing: braided rings squeezed round a shaft by a gland, on valves and slow pumps; it must drip slightly to stay cool.

sections.h3: Gasket joints: seating load and operating load

blocks.text: A gasket seals only after it has been crushed into the roughness of both flanges. The least contact stress that does this is the seating stress y, in MPa. Under pressure the fluid pushes the flanges apart and unloads the gasket, so the bolts must also keep a residual stress of m times the fluid pressure on it; m is the gasket factor. Both come from tables for each material. The pressure vessel code method uses the effective seating width b and the diameter G of the load reaction.

blocks.text: For a flat ring gasket of width N the basic seating width is b₀ = N/2. When b₀ ≤ 6.4 mm, b = b₀ and G is the mean diameter of the gasket; for a wider gasket, b = 2.5√b₀ (mm) and G is the outside contact diameter minus 2b. Then:

blocks.where: W<sub>m2</sub> is the bolt load in N needed to seat the gasket before pressure is applied; b and G in mm; y in MPa.

blocks.text: W<sub>m1</sub> = (π/4) G² p + 2π b G m p
blocks.where: W<sub>m1</sub> is the bolt load in N needed under the design pressure p (MPa). The first term is the end force H of the pressure acting inside G; the second, H<sub>p</sub>, keeps the gasket tight.

blocks.text: The bolts are sized for the larger of the two loads: total bolt core area A<sub>m</sub> = W<sub>m</sub> ÷ σ<sub>b</sub>, with σ<sub>b</sub> the allowable bolt stress. Use an even number of bolts at a close pitch, and tighten them in a criss-cross order so the gasket is crushed evenly.

sections.h3: O-rings, lip seals and face seals

blocks.text: An O-ring seals because it is squeezed: the groove is shallower than the ring section d, and the fluid pressure then pushes the ring against the low-pressure wall of the groove, which tightens the seal. Handbooks give squeeze ranges near 15 to 30 per cent of d for static seals and less for moving ones, to keep friction down. The groove must also leave room for the rubber to spread and swell: the ring section should fill well under about 85 per cent of the groove area. Above roughly 10 MPa, or with a large clearance, a hard backup ring stops the rubber being extruded into the gap.

blocks.where: d is the O-ring cross-section diameter, h the groove depth (the gland depth including any clearance), w the groove width, all in mm.

blocks.text: A lip seal is chosen by shaft diameter and surface speed; the shaft under the lip must be hard and finely ground, and the lip must face the fluid it holds back. Beyond a moderate speed and pressure a mechanical face seal takes over: its leak path is the micron gap between two lapped faces, and the spring and fluid pressure together set the face load.

examples.question: A pressure vessel cover is sealed with a flat compressed-fibre gasket, inside diameter 300 mm and outside diameter 320 mm, with m = 2.00 and y = 11 MPa. The design pressure is 2 MPa and the allowable bolt stress is 138 MPa. Find the seating load, the operating load, the bolt area and a suitable set of bolts.
steps: Gasket width N = (320 − 300)/2 = 10 mm, so b₀ = N/2 = 5 mm. Since 5 ≤ 6.4 mm, b = 5 mm and G = mean diameter = (300 + 320)/2 = 310 mm.
Seating load: W<sub>m2</sub> = π b G y = π × 5 × 310 × 11 = 53 564 N = 53.6 kN.
Pressure end force: H = (π/4) G² p = 0.7854 × 310² × 2 = 150 954 N.
Gasket load under pressure: H<sub>p</sub> = 2π b G m p = 2π × 5 × 310 × 2.00 × 2 = 38 956 N.
Operating load: W<sub>m1</sub> = H + H<sub>p</sub> = 150 954 + 38 956 = 189 910 N = 189.9 kN. This is larger than W<sub>m2</sub>, so it governs.
Bolt area: A<sub>m</sub> = 189 910/138 = 1376 mm². With 16 bolts, each needs 1376/16 = 86.0 mm².
M12 has a stress area of 84.3 mm², too small; M14 has 115 mm². Choose 16 bolts of M14, total 1840 mm².
examples.answer: W<sub>m2</sub> = 53.6 kN, W<sub>m1</sub> = 189.9 kN (governs), A<sub>m</sub> = 1376 mm²; 16 bolts of M14 (1840 mm²) will do.

examples.question: A static O-ring of cross-section d = 3.53 mm sits in a rectangular groove 2.80 mm deep and 4.80 mm wide. Find the squeeze and the groove fill, and say whether the groove is acceptable.
steps: O-ring section area = πd²/4 = π × 3.53²/4 = 9.79 mm².
Check: 21 % squeeze is inside the static range, and 73 % fill is under the 85 % limit.
examples.answer: Squeeze ≈ 21 %, fill ≈ 73 %; the groove is acceptable for a static seal.

traps: Sizing the bolts for the seating load only. They must carry the larger of W<sub>m1</sub> and W<sub>m2</sub>; in the example the pressure case (189.9 kN) governs.
Using the outside diameter for G. For a narrow gasket (b₀ ≤ 6.4 mm) G is the mean diameter of the gasket.
Forgetting the factor 2π in H<sub>p</sub> = 2π b G m p, or putting b = N instead of b₀ = N/2.
Thinking more O-ring squeeze is always better. Too much squeeze, or a groove filled above about 85 %, overloads the rubber and it cracks or extrudes.
Fitting a lip seal with its lip facing away from the oil. The lip must face the fluid it holds back.

quiz.q: Classify seals into static and dynamic, with two examples of each.
quiz.a: Static: gasket, O-ring in a cover groove. Dynamic: lip seal, mechanical face seal, labyrinth seal, gland packing.

quiz.q: Define the gasket factor m and the seating stress y.
quiz.a: y is the least contact stress in MPa that crushes the gasket into the flange roughness and seats it. m is the multiple of the fluid pressure that must remain on the gasket under pressure to keep it tight.

quiz.q: Why does a labyrinth seal suit a steam turbine better than a lip seal?
quiz.a: The labyrinth has no contact, so it does not wear or heat up at high surface speed and temperature. It leaks a little, which a turbine accepts; a rubber lip would burn out.

quiz.q: Why does fluid pressure make an O-ring seal tighter rather than weaker?
quiz.a: The pressure pushes the squeezed ring against the low-pressure wall of the groove, raising its contact stress on the sealing faces above the fluid pressure.

quiz.q: A flat gasket has inside diameter 200 mm, outside diameter 216 mm, and y = 11 MPa. Find the seating load W<sub>m2</sub>.
In the worked example the pressure is doubled to 4 MPa. Which bolt load now governs, and does the bolt choice change?
quiz.a: Both terms of W<sub>m1</sub> double: W<sub>m1</sub> = 2 × 189 910 = 379 820 N, still far above W<sub>m2</sub> = 53 564 N, so it governs. A<sub>m</sub> = 379 820/138 = 2752 mm², 172 mm² for each of 16 bolts, so M14 (115 mm²) and M16 (157 mm²) are too small; use M20 (245 mm²) or more bolts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gasket design is moving from the m and y method to tightness-based methods that set a leak rate the joint must meet. Pumps for toxic liquids use two face seals with a barrier fluid between them. Search next for gasket tightness constants, seal face balance ratio and dry gas seals.
